question: Under FREC Rule 61J2-5.016, a Florida broker's office must consist of, at minimum:
choice_a: A dedicated retail storefront with public parking
choice_b: A minimum of 500 square feet of floor space
choice_c: At least one enclosed room in a building of stationary construction
choice_d: Any mobile trailer registered with the county
explanation: F.A.C. 61J2-5.016 requires a Florida broker's office to consist of at least one enclosed room in a building of stationary construction, ensuring the office is a fixed, identifiable place of business.

question: May a Florida sales associate or broker associate personally own a real estate brokerage entity?
choice_a: No, only a licensed broker may have any ownership interest in a brokerage
choice_b: Yes, with no restriction on the role held
choice_c: Only if the sales associate has at least 10 years of experience
choice_d: Yes, but the sales associate or broker associate may not be registered as that brokerage's officer, director, or general partner
explanation: F.A.C. 61J2-5.016 permits a sales associate or broker associate to own a brokerage entity, but they may not serve as its officer, director, or general partner -- those governance roles are reserved for licensed brokers who can be held accountable for the entity's real estate activity.

question: If a Florida brokerage maintains multiple branch offices across the state, those branch offices must:
choice_a: Operate under the same corporate or trade name as the primary office, regardless of geographic location
choice_b: Each independently register a completely different trade name
choice_c: Be limited to no more than two branch offices statewide
choice_d: Operate without any broker or broker associate physically overseeing them
explanation: FREC rules require that all branch offices of a Florida brokerage operate under the same corporate or trade name as the principal office, no matter where in the state they are located, preserving consistent brand and licensure accountability.

question: A registered brokerage entity formed as a sole proprietorship, general partnership, limited partnership, limited liability partnership, or corporation is distinguished under Florida law from:
choice_c: A brokerage licensed only in another state
choice_d: A brokerage with no sales associates
explanation: The broker exam content outline distinguishes registered brokerage entities (sole proprietorships, general partnerships, limited partnerships, LLPs, corporations) from non-registered entities, a distinction with real consequences for how the entity may lawfully conduct brokerage business in Florida.
source_note: DBPR Real Estate Broker Candidate Information Booklet, Content Overview and Outline, Section I.B.1-2

question: A broker operating under a name other than their own licensed legal name is generally required to register that name as a:
choice_a: Trademark with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office only
choice_b: DBA filed solely with the IRS
choice_c: Trade (fictitious) name, consistent with Florida's Fictitious Name Act
choice_d: Nothing -- trade names require no registration in Florida
explanation: Operating under a business name other than the broker's own legal name generally requires registration consistent with Section 865.09, F.S. (Florida's Fictitious Name Act), and that registered trade name must also be properly reflected on the broker's DBPR license records.
source_note: Section 865.09, F.S. (Fictitious Name Act); DBPR Real Estate Broker Candidate Information Booklet, Printable Law Booklet reference list, item 39

question: Since FREC Rule 61J2-10.024 (Office Entrance Signs) was repealed, the requirement that a broker maintain a proper office entrance sign is now governed by:
choice_c: No statute currently addresses office signage
explanation: Although the specific administrative rule on office entrance signs (61J2-10.024) was repealed, the underlying obligation to display a proper broker office sign is addressed through Section 475.22(1), F.S., and failure to maintain it remains a compliance issue.
source_note: Section 475.22(1), F.S.; F.A.C. 61J2-10.024 (repealed, superseded by statute)

question: A broker's office must generally comply with which federal accessibility law when the office is open to the public?
choice_c: The Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act
explanation: A brokerage office open to the public falls within the scope of the Americans with Disabilities Act's public-accommodation requirements, an item the broker exam content outline lists under Office Requirements.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. Section 12101 et seq. (ADA); DBPR Real Estate Broker Candidate Information Booklet, Content Overview and Outline, Section I.B.4.d

question: A real estate advertisement that fails to identify the involvement of a real estate licensee or brokerage, appearing to be placed by a private individual or unlicensed party, is commonly known as a:
explanation: A 'blind ad' is real estate advertising that conceals the fact a licensed broker or sales associate is involved; Florida law and FREC rules generally prohibit blind advertising because consumers are entitled to know they are dealing with a licensee.
source_note: F.A.C. 61J2-10.025 (Advertising); DBPR Real Estate Broker Candidate Information Booklet, Content Overview and Outline, Section I.B.5.b

question: Under Florida advertising rules, an advertisement placed by a sales associate for a listing must:
choice_a: Only display the sales associate's personal cell phone number
choice_b: Never mention the sales associate's name at all
choice_c: Disclose the name of the brokerage under which the sales associate is registered
choice_d: Be approved in writing by DBPR before publication
explanation: Florida advertising rules require that any advertisement by a sales associate disclose the brokerage's name, since the sales associate's authority to advertise and negotiate flows through their broker; failing to identify the brokerage misleads the public and can constitute a false/misleading advertising violation.

question: Real estate advertising that violates the Fair Housing Act's prohibition on discriminatory language, such as indicating a preference based on race, religion, or familial status, exposes a broker to:
choice_a: No consequence, since advertising is a purely business decision
choice_b: Only a private civil claim, with no regulatory exposure
choice_c: Liability solely for the sales associate who placed the ad, never the broker
choice_d: Both federal Fair Housing Act liability and FREC disciplinary action
explanation: Discriminatory real estate advertising can trigger liability under the federal Fair Housing Act (42 U.S.C. Section 3601 et seq.) as well as FREC discipline for violating Florida license law's advertising and anti-discrimination standards; a broker's supervisory responsibility for office advertising means broker-level exposure is real, not limited to the associate who drafted the ad.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. Section 3601 et seq. (Fair Housing Act); DBPR Real Estate Broker Candidate Information Booklet, Content Overview and Outline, Section I.B.5.c

question: A broker's telephone solicitation practices for prospecting new listings are subject to which additional layer of compliance beyond FREC advertising rules?
choice_a: The federal Telephone Consumer Protection Act and Do-Not-Call regulations
choice_b: No additional compliance layer beyond ordinary advertising rules
explanation: Beyond FREC's own advertising standards, brokers engaging in telephone solicitation must also comply with federal Do-Not-Call and Telephone Consumer Protection Act requirements, a topic the broker content outline lists directly under Advertising.
source_note: DBPR Real Estate Broker Candidate Information Booklet, Content Overview and Outline, Section I.B.5.d; federal Telephone Consumer Protection Act

question: A brokerage that compiles and sells lists of available rental properties to prospective tenants for a fee must comply with Florida's specific statutory requirements governing:
explanation: Florida law separately regulates rental list businesses that charge advance fees for lists of available rentals (Section 475.01(1)(c) definitions and related provisions), and the broker exam content outline lists rental lists as a distinct brokerage-entity compliance topic.
source_note: Section 475.01, F.S.; DBPR Real Estate Broker Candidate Information Booklet, Content Overview and Outline, Section I.B.5.e

question: A corporation registered as a Florida brokerage entity must designate a licensed broker to serve as:
choice_a: A silent, unlicensed investor with no operational role
choice_b: An outside accountant reviewing only tax filings
choice_c: The entity's qualifying broker, responsible for supervising the entity's real estate activity
choice_d: A part-time consultant with no licensure requirement
explanation: A brokerage corporation (or other registered entity) must have a licensed broker serving as its qualifying broker -- the individual through whom the entity's real estate license operates and who bears supervisory responsibility for the entity's licensed activity.

question: A limited liability partnership (LLP) registering as a Florida brokerage entity is governed, in addition to Chapter 475, by which other body of Florida statutory law?
explanation: A brokerage entity organized as a partnership form, including an LLP, is subject to Chapter 620, F.S. (Partnership Laws) in addition to the real estate licensing requirements of Chapter 475 -- one of the general business-entity statutes the DBPR candidate booklet's reference list flags as relevant to brokerage entity structuring.
source_note: Chapter 620, F.S.; DBPR Real Estate Broker Candidate Information Booklet, Printable Law Booklet reference list, item 22

question: A brokerage organized as a Florida limited liability company (LLC) is primarily governed, apart from Chapter 475, by:
choice_b: Chapter 617, Florida Statutes (Corporations Not For Profit)
choice_c: Chapter 721, Florida Statutes (Vacation and Timeshare Plans)
explanation: Florida LLCs, including brokerage entities organized in that form, are governed by Chapter 605, F.S., in addition to the licensure requirements applicable to any registered brokerage entity under Chapter 475.
source_note: Chapter 605, F.S.; DBPR Real Estate Broker Candidate Information Booklet, Printable Law Booklet reference list, item 17

question: A brokerage that fails to properly register its trade (fictitious) name before advertising under it risks:
choice_a: No consequence, since fictitious name registration is optional in Florida
choice_b: FREC disciplinary exposure for a licensure/advertising violation, in addition to any Fictitious Name Act noncompliance
choice_c: Automatic revocation of the broker's license with no opportunity to correct it
choice_d: Criminal prosecution only, with no administrative exposure
explanation: Advertising or operating under an unregistered trade name exposes a broker both to noncompliance with the Fictitious Name Act (Section 865.09, F.S.) and to FREC disciplinary action for advertising/licensure violations, since the brokerage's licensed name of record must match how it holds itself out to the public.
source_note: Section 865.09, F.S.; F.A.C. 61J2-10 (Operation, Business and Offices)
